topics.title: The role of accounting and types of business
points: Accounting collects and records financial data, then reports, analyses and interprets it to help people make decisions.
Users include the owner, lenders, suppliers, the ATO, employees and potential investors.
Financial data is the raw facts about transactions; financial information is that data sorted and summarised so it is useful.
Ownership structures: sole trader (one owner), partnership (two or more), private company (shareholders, a separate legal entity).
Sources of finance: owner’s capital (internal) or borrowing such as loans, overdrafts and trade credit (external).
topics.explain: Explain to a friend who wants to open a market stall why they should keep accounting records, and who else might want to see them.

p: You need nothing before this lesson: it is the starting point for accounting.

The big idea: every business needs answers to a few questions. Are we making a profit? Can we pay our bills? What do we own and owe? Accounting is the system that produces those answers. This lesson explains what accounting is for, who uses it, and the basic choices an owner makes when starting a business.

The accounting process has four steps. Source documents are collected as evidence of each transaction. The data is recorded and sorted. Reports summarise it. The reports are then analysed and interpreted to give advice.

A transaction is an exchange between the business and another party that can be measured in dollars, such as selling goods, paying wages or borrowing money. Financial data is the raw detail on documents. Financial information is the result of processing that data into a form a person can use to make a decision. A shoebox of receipts is data; an Income Statement is information.
check: What is the difference between financial data and financial information?
Data is the raw facts and figures from transactions. Information is data that has been sorted, summarised and reported so it can be used to make decisions.

fig.cap: The four steps of the accounting process.

p: The owner uses it to decide prices, control costs, judge whether to expand and check that the business can pay its debts. A bank uses it to decide whether to lend and whether the loan can be repaid. Suppliers use it to decide whether to offer credit. The Australian Taxation Office uses it to check that the right amount of tax and GST is paid. Employees care whether the business can keep paying wages. A potential buyer or investor uses it to decide what the business is worth.
Each user needs different information, but all of them rely on the reports being prepared in a consistent, honest way.

By activity: a service business sells time and skill (a plumber, a tutor); a trading business buys goods and resells them (a clothing shop); a manufacturing business makes goods. Units 1 and 2 begin with service businesses and move to trading businesses.

By ownership. A sole trader is owned and run by one person. It is cheap and simple to set up and the owner keeps all the profit and makes all the decisions, but the owner has unlimited liability: personal assets such as a house can be used to pay business debts. A partnership has two or more owners who share capital, skills, workload and profit; it also has unlimited liability and can suffer from disputes. A private company is a separate legal entity owned by shareholders, who have limited liability: they can lose only what they invested. Companies cost more to set up and have more reporting requirements.
check: What does unlimited liability mean for a sole trader?
The owner is personally responsible for all business debts, so personal assets can be used to pay them.

p: Internal finance comes from the owner (capital contributions) or from profits kept in the business. It has no interest cost and no repayments, but it is limited by the owner’s wealth.

External finance is borrowed. A bank loan gives a fixed amount repaid over a set time with interest. A bank overdraft lets the business overdraw its account up to a limit, which is flexible but usually has a higher interest rate. Trade credit is buying from suppliers now and paying later. Borrowing allows growth without the owner contributing more, but interest must be paid and the debt repaid whether or not the business is doing well, which adds risk.

Before starting or buying a business, an owner weighs the expected return against the risk and against alternatives. If $100,000 invested in the business is expected to earn $8,000 profit a year, the return is 8%. If a bank term deposit pays 5% with almost no risk, the owner must decide whether an extra 3% is enough reward for the risk and the work. Non-financial factors count as well: being your own boss, hours of work, and the effect on the community and environment.

Mixing up the owner and the business; they are treated as separate in accounting even for a sole trader. Saying a sole trader has limited liability. Describing accounting as only “recording”: the purpose is to provide information for decisions. Treating loans and capital as the same thing.

qs.q: Which is an advantage of operating as a sole trader?
o: The owner keeps all profits and control
Easier to raise large amounts of capital

qs.q: A bank deciding whether to approve a loan is most interested in the business’s…
qs.e: Lenders look at liquidity, stability and existing debt.

qs.q: Which is an external source of finance?
List the four steps of the accounting process.
qs.a: Source documents, recording, reporting, and advice (analysis and interpretation).

qs.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of a partnership compared with a sole trader.
qs.a: Advantage: more capital, shared skills and workload. Disadvantage: profits are shared, decisions can cause disputes, and partners still have unlimited liability.

qs.q: Shareholders of a private company have…
qs.e: They can lose only the amount they invested.

qs.q: Which is an internal source of finance?
o: A capital contribution from the owner

qs.q: Name two users of a business’s accounting reports and what each wants to know.
qs.a: For example: the owner (is the business profitable?) and a bank (can the business repay a loan?).

topics.title: The accounting equation and the elements
points: Assets = Liabilities + Owner’s Equity. The equation always balances.
Assets are resources the business controls; liabilities are what it owes to outsiders; owner’s equity is what is left for the owner.
Revenue increases owner’s equity; expenses decrease it. Profit = revenue − expenses.
Every transaction changes at least two items, keeping the equation in balance.
Capital contributions and drawings change owner’s equity but are not revenue or expenses.
topics.explain: Use the accounting equation to explain why buying a van with a bank loan does not make the owner any richer.

p: Before this lesson you should know what a transaction is and that the business is treated as separate from its owner.

The big idea: everything a business has was paid for by someone, either by lenders and suppliers or by the owner. That one idea, written as an equation, is the foundation of all accounting. If you can work out how a transaction changes the equation, you understand the transaction.

Assets are economic resources controlled by the business that are expected to bring it benefits: cash at bank, inventory, amounts owed by customers (Accounts Receivable), vehicles, equipment, premises.
Liabilities are obligations to hand over resources to someone outside the business: amounts owed to suppliers (Accounts Payable), loans, GST owed to the ATO.

Owner’s equity is the owner’s claim on the assets: what would be left if all assets were used to pay all liabilities. It is increased by capital contributions and profit, and decreased by drawings and losses.

Revenue is what the business earns from its activities, such as sales or fees, which increases owner’s equity. Expenses are what it consumes in earning that revenue, such as wages, rent and the cost of goods sold, which decreases owner’s equity.
check: Classify each as an asset, liability or owner’s equity: inventory; bank loan; capital; Accounts Payable.
Inventory is an asset. The bank loan and Accounts Payable are liabilities. Capital is owner’s equity.

p: Assets = Liabilities + Owner’s Equity. Rearranged: Owner’s Equity = Assets − Liabilities.

Example: a business has cash $5,000, inventory $12,000 and a van worth $18,000, and it owes a supplier $4,000 and the bank $10,000. Assets = $35,000. Liabilities = $14,000. Owner’s equity = 35,000 − 14,000 = $21,000.

fig.cap: The accounting equation as a balance: everything the business has (assets) was funded by outsiders (liabilities) or the owner (owner’s equity).

p: For each transaction ask: which items change, and does each go up or down? Then check that the equation still balances.

1. Owner contributes $20,000 cash. Bank (asset) +20,000; Capital (owner’s equity) +20,000. 2. Buys equipment for $6,000 cash. Equipment +6,000; Bank −6,000. Total assets unchanged. 3. Buys inventory for $3,000 on credit. Inventory +3,000; Accounts Payable (liability) +3,000. 4. Pays the supplier $1,000. Bank −1,000; Accounts Payable −1,000. 5. Earns fees of $2,500 in cash. Bank +2,500; owner’s equity +2,500 (revenue). 6. Pays wages $800. Bank −800; owner’s equity −800 (expense). 7. Owner withdraws $300. Bank −300; owner’s equity −300 (drawings).
check: A business takes out a $15,000 bank loan. What happens to the accounting equation?
Assets (Bank) increase by $15,000 and liabilities (Loan) increase by $15,000. Owner’s equity does not change.
A business pays $400 for advertising. Which two items change?
Bank (an asset) decreases by $400 and owner’s equity decreases by $400, because advertising is an expense.

notes.h: Revenue and expenses are not the same as cash
p: Revenue is earned when the goods or service are provided, even if the customer pays later. An expense is incurred when the benefit is consumed, even if it is paid later. A cash payment to buy a van is not an expense: one asset (cash) is swapped for another (the van). A loan received is not revenue: the business has more cash but owes the same amount. Keeping these distinctions clear prevents most errors in reports.

Current assets are expected to be turned into cash, sold or used up within 12 months: bank, Accounts Receivable, inventory, prepaid expenses. Non-current assets will be used for longer: vehicles, equipment, premises. Current liabilities are due within 12 months: Accounts Payable, GST, the next year’s loan repayments. Non-current liabilities are due later. The classification shows whether the business can meet its short-term debts.

Treating a capital contribution as revenue or drawings as an expense. Treating the purchase of an asset as an expense. Forgetting that every transaction has two effects. Thinking owner’s equity is cash: it is a claim on all the assets, most of which are not cash.

qs.q: Assets are $80,000 and liabilities are $30,000. Owner’s equity is…
A business buys office furniture for $2,000 cash. The effect on the accounting equation is…
o: assets increase and decrease by the same amount
qs.e: Furniture rises and Bank falls; total assets do not change.

qs.q: Which transaction decreases owner’s equity?
o: Collecting cash from a customer who owed money

qs.q: Why are drawings not an expense?
qs.a: Drawings are assets taken by the owner for personal use. They are not consumed in earning revenue, so they reduce owner’s equity directly without affecting profit.

qs.q: State the accounting equation and explain why it always balances.
qs.a: Assets = Liabilities + Owner’s Equity. Every asset is funded either by outsiders (liabilities) or by the owner (owner’s equity), and every transaction has two equal effects.

qs.q: A customer pays $500 they owed from last month. The effect is…
qs.e: The revenue was recorded when the sale was made. Now one asset replaces another.

qs.q: A business has assets of $50,000 and liabilities of $18,000. What is owner’s equity?
The owner takes home inventory that cost $500. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
qs.a: Assets (inventory) decrease by $500 and owner’s equity decreases by $500 (drawings).

topics.title: Source documents and GST
points: The four steps of accounting: source documents → records → reports → advice.
Tax invoice: a credit sale or purchase (Sales or Purchases Journal). Receipt or till tape: cash received. Cheque butt, EFT or payroll: cash paid.
Credit note: goods returned or a price reduction. Bank statement: the bank’s record, used for bank reconciliation. Memo: internal (drawings of stock, depreciation).
GST is 10%: GST = price × 10% = GST-inclusive total ÷ 11.
No GST on wages, capital, drawings, loan principal or interest.
GST payable = GST collected on sales − GST paid on purchases. If negative, it is a GST receivable (refund).
topics.explain: Explain why the business must keep a source document for every transaction.

qs.q: Which document proves a credit sale?
A tax invoice total is $3 300 including GST. Find the GST and the price.
Which payment has no GST?
GST collected is $700 and GST paid is $900. What is the GST position?
qs.a: GST receivable (refund due) of $200, a current asset.

qs.q: A tax invoice shows a total of $1,320 including GST. Find the GST and the amount before GST.
qs.a: GST $120; $1,200 before GST

qs.q: Which source document records cash received?
For a quarter, GST collected on sales is $2,500 and GST paid on purchases is $1,800. What is the result?
qs.a: $700 owed to the ATO (GST settlement)

qs.q: GST does not apply to…

p: Before this lesson you should know the accounting equation and the five elements (assets, liabilities, owner’s equity, revenue and expenses) from the first two lessons.

The big idea: accounting is a process with four steps. Source documents provide the evidence, records sort and summarise it, reports present it, and advice is given to the owner based on the reports. This lesson covers the first step and the tax that sits on most documents, GST.

A source document is the paper or electronic evidence that a transaction happened. Nothing is recorded without one. This is what makes accounting information verifiable: anyone checking the records can trace each figure back to its evidence, which supports faithful representation.

Each document tells you four things: the date, the other party, what was exchanged, and the amounts including any GST. In the exam, read the document before deciding the journal. Ask two questions: was cash exchanged now, and is this business the seller or the buyer?

Cash receipt or EFTPOS summary: cash came in (cash sale, capital contribution, loan received, receipt from an Account Receivable). Recorded in the Cash Receipts Journal. Cheque butt, EFT or bank transfer record: cash went out (cash purchase, wages, payment to an Account Payable, drawings, loan repayment). Recorded in the Cash Payments Journal.

Sales invoice (a tax invoice this business issued): a credit sale, recorded in the Sales Journal. Purchase invoice (a tax invoice this business received): a credit purchase of inventory, recorded in the Purchases Journal. Credit note: a return or allowance on a credit transaction. Memo: an internal document for transactions with no outside party, such as the owner taking inventory home, correcting an error, or a balance day adjustment.
To tell a sales invoice from a purchase invoice, look at whose name is at the top. The business named at the top is the seller.

GST is a 10% tax on most goods and services. A business registered for GST acts as a collector for the Australian Taxation Office. It charges GST on its sales (a liability, because it owes that money to the ATO) and pays GST on its purchases (which it can claim back, reducing the liability). GST is never revenue and never an expense for a registered business.

If GST on sales is greater than GST on purchases, the business has a GST liability and makes a GST settlement to the ATO. If GST on purchases is greater, the business is owed a GST refund, and the balance is a current asset.
check: A business makes a cash sale for $550 including GST. How much is revenue and how much is GST?
GST = 550 ÷ 11 = $50. Sales revenue = $500.

p: A business sells goods on credit for $660 including GST, and buys inventory for cash for $330 including GST.

Sale: GST = 660 ÷ 11 = $60; Sales revenue = $600; Account Receivable increases by $660. Purchase: GST = 330 ÷ 11 = $30; Inventory increases by $300; Bank decreases by $330. Net GST owed to the ATO = 60 − 30 = $30.

notes.h: Reading a document, step by step
p: Take any document and answer five questions. What type is it? Who issued it, and are we the seller or the buyer? What is the date? What was exchanged? What are the amounts: before GST, GST, and total?

Example: a tax invoice headed “Beach Boards”, addressed to “Surf Shack”, dated 4 March, for 5 surfboards at $400 each plus GST $200, total $2,200, terms 30 days. If we are Surf Shack, this is a credit purchase of inventory: Inventory increases by $2,000, the GST of $200 can be claimed back, and we owe Beach Boards $2,200 as an Account Payable. If we are Beach Boards, the same document is a credit sale: Sales revenue $2,000, GST $200 owed to the ATO, and an Account Receivable of $2,200.
One document is always two-sided. Deciding which side you are on is the most important step.
check: Your business receives a tax invoice from a supplier for inventory, with 14-day terms. Is this a cash or credit transaction, and which journal would record it?
A credit purchase of inventory, recorded in the Purchases Journal.

p: At the end of each reporting period for GST, the business totals the GST it charged customers and the GST it paid suppliers.

Example: during a quarter a shop makes sales of $44,000 including GST and purchases and pays expenses of $27,500 including GST. GST on sales = 44,000 ÷ 11 = $4,000. GST on purchases = 27,500 ÷ 11 = $2,500. The business owes the ATO 4,000 − 2,500 = $1,500. Until it is paid, that $1,500 is a current liability. When it is paid, the payment is called a GST settlement.

If the shop had bought a $33,000 delivery van that quarter as well, GST on purchases would rise by $3,000 to $5,500. GST paid would then exceed GST collected by $1,500, and the business would be owed a GST refund, a current asset until received.
check: GST on sales is $3,200 and GST on purchases is $4,100. What is the result?
The business paid $900 more than it collected, so it is owed a GST refund of $900 (a current asset).

notes.h: Why documents matter for the quality of information
p: A document is evidence that can be checked by someone else, which makes the information verifiable. Because the amount comes from the document and not from someone’s opinion, the information is free from bias, which supports faithful representation. Documents are numbered and filed so that every entry in the records can be traced back.

Calculating 10% of a GST-inclusive figure. Divide by 11 when the amount includes GST; multiply by 10% only when it excludes GST. Recording GST as part of Sales or Inventory. Adding GST to wages, drawings, loan repayments or the owner’s capital contribution; none of these attract GST.

topics.title: The four journals
points: Cash Receipts Journal: Bank, Sales, Receipts from Accounts Receivable, Sundries, GST.
Cash Payments Journal: Bank, Inventory, Accounts Payable, Drawings, Wages, Sundries, GST.
Sales Journal: Sales, GST, Accounts Receivable. Purchases Journal: Inventory, GST, Accounts Payable.
Sundries is for anything without its own column; write the account name in Details.
The Bank (or total) column must equal the sum of the other columns.
Receipts from AR and payments to AP carry no GST in the cash journals: it was recorded at the credit transaction.
topics.explain: Explain how an EFT payment for rent of $1 100 is recorded, column by column.

qs.q: Record a cash sale of $4 400 (incl. GST) in the Cash Receipts Journal.
qs.a: Bank 4 400, Sales 4 000, GST 400

qs.q: An owner contributes $20 000 cash. Which column is used besides Bank?
A customer pays $2 000 they owe. Which columns are used?
qs.e: No GST: it was recorded on the original invoice.

qs.q: Record a $6 600 credit purchase of inventory (incl. GST) in the Purchases Journal.
qs.a: Inventory 6 000, GST 600, Accounts Payable 6 600

qs.q: A credit sale of inventory is recorded in the…
Record a cash sale of $330 including GST, with a cost of $180, in the Cash Receipts Journal columns.
qs.a: Bank 330; Sales 300; GST 30; Cost of Sales 180
s: Cost of Sales (from the inventory card) = 180; it is not part of the Bank total.

qs.q: A payment to a supplier for goods bought on credit last month is recorded in the Cash Payments Journal under…
Why is there no GST on a receipt from an Account Receivable?
qs.a: The GST was recorded when the credit sale was made; the receipt only collects the debt.

p: Before this lesson you should be able to identify source documents and calculate GST (previous lesson).

The big idea: a business may have hundreds of transactions a month. Journals sort them by type and add them up, so the owner works with a few totals instead of hundreds of separate entries. If you can choose the right journal and the right column, you can record almost any transaction.

Journals are the first place transactions are recorded. They gather transactions of the same type in date order and total them, so only the totals need to be carried to the next stage. Special journals (the cash and credit journals) handle the frequent transactions; the General Journal handles the rest.

Choosing the journal is a two-step decision. Was cash received or paid at the time? If yes, use a cash journal. If the transaction was on credit, was it a sale of inventory (Sales Journal) or a purchase of inventory (Purchases Journal)?

Each special journal has a total column and classification columns. Frequent items have their own column so one total can be used later. Infrequent items go in Sundries with the account named in the details column.

In the Cash Receipts Journal a cash sale needs two things recorded: the selling price, and the cost of the inventory that left the shelf (a Cost of Sales column, taken from the inventory card). The cost price never includes GST. In the Sales Journal the same applies: Sales and GST make up the Account Receivable total, and Cost of Sales is recorded separately at cost.

notes.h: Why receipts from customers carry no GST
p: GST is recorded once, when the sale or purchase occurs. A credit sale of $1,100 records $100 GST on the day of the invoice. When the customer pays three weeks later, the business is only collecting a debt, so the Cash Receipts Journal shows $1,100 in the Accounts Receivable column and nothing in GST. Recording GST again would double-count it.
check: A customer pays $1,100 owing from a credit sale last month. What goes in the GST column of the Cash Receipts Journal?
Nothing. The GST was recorded in the Sales Journal when the sale was made.

p: Transactions: 3 May cash sale $440 incl. GST (cost $250); 5 May credit sale to J. Li $880 incl. GST (cost $500); 9 May received $880 from J. Li; 12 May owner contributed $5,000 cash.

Cash Receipts Journal: 3 May Bank 440, Sales 400, GST 40, Cost of Sales 250. 9 May Bank 880, Accounts Receivable 880. 12 May Bank 5,000, Sundries 5,000 (Capital). Sales Journal: 5 May Sales 800, GST 80, Accounts Receivable 880, Cost of Sales 500.
Check: in each cash journal row, the Bank amount equals the sum of the other columns except Cost of Sales, which is a memo of the cost and is not cash.

notes.h: A decision path for any transaction
p: Question 1: was cash received at the time? If yes, Cash Receipts Journal. Question 2: was cash paid at the time? If yes, Cash Payments Journal. Question 3: was it a credit sale of inventory? Sales Journal. Question 4: was it a credit purchase of inventory? Purchases Journal. Anything else, such as a credit purchase of equipment, the owner taking inventory home, or correcting an error, goes in the General Journal.

Examples: paid wages $900 (Cash Payments Journal; no GST). Received $330 from a customer who bought on credit last month (Cash Receipts Journal; Accounts Receivable column; no GST). Bought inventory for $1,100 on credit (Purchases Journal). Owner withdrew $200 cash (Cash Payments Journal; Drawings; no GST). Paid $660 for advertising including GST (Cash Payments Journal; Advertising $600, GST $60).
check: The business buys a computer on credit for use in the office. Which journal is used?
The General Journal. The Purchases Journal is only for credit purchases of inventory.

fig.cap: Which journal? Ask these questions in order.

notes.h: Worked example: Cash Payments Journal and Purchases Journal
p: Transactions: 2 June paid rent $1,320 including GST. 6 June bought inventory on credit from Kelp Co. for $2,200 including GST. 15 June paid Kelp Co. $2,200. 20 June bought inventory for cash $550 including GST. 28 June owner withdrew $400.

Cash Payments Journal: 2 June Bank 1,320; Sundries 1,200 (Rent); GST 120. 15 June Bank 2,200; Accounts Payable 2,200. 20 June Bank 550; Inventory 500; GST 50. 28 June Bank 400; Drawings 400. Totals: Bank 4,470; Inventory 500; Accounts Payable 2,200; Drawings 400; Sundries 1,200; GST 170. Check: 500 + 2,200 + 400 + 1,200 + 170 = 4,470.
Purchases Journal: 6 June Kelp Co.; Inventory 2,000; GST 200; Accounts Payable 2,200.
check: A business pays $2,750 including GST for inventory. What amounts go in the Bank, Inventory and GST columns?
Bank $2,750; Inventory $2,500; GST $250.

notes.h: From journals to the rest of the system
p: At the end of the period each column is totalled. The totals show the owner, for example, total cash received and paid, total credit sales and how much was spent on each type of expense. These totals feed the reports: the cash journals supply the Cash Flow Statement, and the sales, cost of sales and expense totals supply the Income Statement. In Units 3 and 4 the totals are posted to ledger accounts using double entry.

Including Cost of Sales when cross-adding to Bank. Recording a credit purchase of a non-current asset in the Purchases Journal: that journal is only for inventory bought on credit; other credit purchases go in the General Journal. Forgetting the document number, which is the evidence that supports verifiability.

map: Cost of Sales is a memo
none on AR receipts or AP payments

topics.title: Inventory cards
points: Inventory cards have IN, OUT and BALANCE columns (quantity, unit cost, total), at cost price, GST excluded.
Cost of Sales = inventory sold (OUT) at cost. Identified cost uses each item’s actual cost; FIFO assumes the oldest stock sells first.
A stocktake (physical count) checks the cards. Card higher than count = inventory loss (expense); lower = inventory gain (revenue).
The Balance Sheet shows inventory at the physical count.
Drawings of inventory by the owner are recorded at cost and are not an expense.
topics.explain: Explain why inventory sold is recorded at cost, not selling price, on the card.

qs.q: Card balance is $1 800; the stocktake counts $1 750. What is recorded?

At what value are entries recorded on an inventory card?
qs.a: At cost price, excluding GST.

qs.q: Identified Cost is most suitable for…
o: distinguishable, high-value items such as cars
identical low-cost items such as screws

p: Before this lesson you should understand source documents, GST and the journals.

The big idea: for a business that buys and sells goods, inventory is usually its most important asset and Cost of Sales its largest expense. An inventory card tracks both. Every figure on the card is at cost price, because the card records what the business paid, not what it hopes to earn.

A trading business buys goods and sells them at a higher price. Under the perpetual system, an inventory card is kept for each line and updated after every movement, so the business always knows how many units it should have and what they cost. The cards feed two figures into the reports: Cost of Sales (an expense in the Income Statement) and Inventory on hand (a current asset in the Balance Sheet).

Units of the same product are often bought at different prices, so the business needs a rule for which cost to use when units are sold. Identified Cost tracks each unit individually (by a code or serial number) and uses that unit’s actual cost; it suits expensive, distinguishable items such as cars or jewellery. First In First Out assumes the earliest units bought are the first sold; it suits identical items where tracking each one is impractical.

Under FIFO, when costs are rising, Cost of Sales uses the older, cheaper costs. That gives a lower Cost of Sales and a higher Gross Profit, and the units left on hand are valued at the most recent costs.

Purchases go IN at cost (excluding GST). Sales go OUT at cost price, never at selling price. A sales return comes back IN at the cost at which it went out. A purchase return goes OUT at the cost at which it came in. Drawings of inventory and inventory used for advertising go OUT at cost.

A physical count is done at least once a period to check that the cards match reality. Differences come from theft, damage, breakage, recording errors, or supplying the wrong quantity. An inventory loss is recorded in the OUT column and reported as an expense; an inventory gain is recorded in the IN column and reported as revenue. After the adjustment, the card balance equals the count.
check: The card shows 40 units and the stocktake counts 38. What is recorded?
An inventory loss of 2 units, in the OUT column, reported as an expense.

p: 1 Mar balance 10 units at $20. 6 Mar purchase 20 units at $22. 10 Mar sale of 15 units. 31 Mar stocktake counts 14 units.

10 Mar OUT: 10 at $20 = $200 and 5 at $22 = $110, so Cost of Sales = $310. Balance: 15 at $22 = $330. 31 Mar: the card shows 15 and the count is 14, so there is an inventory loss of 1 unit at $22 = $22. Closing balance: 14 at $22 = $308.

The heading names the item, its supplier, its location and the cost assignment method. The body has a date column, a details column with the document number, and three sections, IN, OUT and BALANCE, each split into quantity, unit cost and total value. After every transaction the BALANCE is rewritten, keeping different unit costs on separate lines.
Documents drive the entries: a purchase invoice or cheque butt (IN), a sales invoice or receipt (OUT), a credit note (returns), and a memo (drawings, losses and gains).
check: At what value is a sale recorded in an inventory card?
At cost price, in the OUT column. The selling price never appears on the card.

p: A bike shop tags each bike. On hand at 1 May: bike A1 cost $300 and bike A2 cost $320. On 5 May it buys bikes B1 and B2 at $350 each. On 9 May it sells bikes A2 and B1.
Cost of Sales on 9 May = 320 + 350 = $670. Balance: A1 at $300 and B2 at $350, total $650. The cost follows the actual item sold, so there is no assumption about order.

notes.h: Worked example: FIFO with a return
p: 1 July balance 20 units at $10. 4 July purchase 30 units at $12. 10 July sale of 35 units. 12 July the customer returns 2 of those units. 20 July owner takes 3 units for personal use.

10 July OUT: 20 at $10 and 15 at $12 = 200 + 180 = $380. Balance: 15 at $12. 12 July sales return IN: the 2 units come back at the cost of the last units to leave on that sale, $12, so IN 2 at $12 = $24. Balance: 17 at $12. 20 July drawings OUT: 3 at $12 = $36. Balance: 14 at $12 = $168.
Cost of Sales for the month = 380 − 24 = $356. Drawings of $36 reduce owner’s equity; they are not part of Cost of Sales.
check: Balance: 5 units at $8 and 10 units at $9. Under FIFO, what is the Cost of Sales for a sale of 8 units?

p: Identified Cost is the most accurate, since every unit is matched with its real cost, but it needs each unit to be labelled and tracked, which is only practical for individually distinguishable or high-value items. FIFO is easier for identical items and leaves the inventory on hand valued at the most recent costs. Whichever method is chosen should be used consistently, so that results can be compared from one period to the next (comparability).

Using the selling price in the card. Including GST in the unit cost. Under FIFO, taking all the units from the latest batch. Showing the balance as one blended line when two cost prices are still on hand; keep each cost on its own line.

topics.title: AR, AP, depreciation and double entry
points: One AR record per customer and one AP record per supplier; schedules total them to the Balance Sheet figure.
AR = opening + credit sales (incl. GST) − receipts − returns. AP = opening + credit purchases (incl. GST) − payments − returns.
Straight-line depreciation = (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life. Reducing balance = carrying amount × rate.
Carrying amount = cost − accumulated depreciation. Depreciation is an expense but not a cash flow.
Double entry: assets, expenses and drawings increase with a debit; liabilities, capital and revenue increase with a credit.

p: Before this lesson you should be able to record credit transactions in the Sales and Purchases Journals.

The big idea: selling on credit and buying on credit help a business trade, but both must be managed, and assets that last for years must have their cost spread over the years they are used. This lesson covers the records and calculations behind Accounts Receivable, Accounts Payable and non-current assets.

The Balance Sheet shows one figure for Accounts Receivable and one for Accounts Payable. To manage credit the business also needs to know who owes what. A separate record is kept for each customer and each supplier. The total of the individual balances must equal the single figure reported, and that check helps detect errors.

notes.h: Managing Accounts Receivable and Accounts Payable
p: Credit sales increase sales but delay cash and bring the risk that a customer never pays. Good management includes credit checks before offering credit, clear credit terms on invoices, prompt invoicing, reminder notices, discounts for early payment and stopping credit for slow payers.
For Accounts Payable the aim is to pay on time but not early, unless a discount makes early payment worthwhile. Paying late damages the relationship with suppliers and may lose credit facilities.

A non-current asset is used for more than 12 months to help earn revenue. Its cost is everything needed to get it ready for use: purchase price (excluding GST), delivery, installation and modifications. Depreciation spreads the depreciable amount over the asset’s useful life, so that each period carries a share of the cost as an expense. It is an allocation of cost, not a valuation and not a saving of cash.

Straight-line gives the same expense each year and suits assets that contribute evenly. Reducing balance gives a higher expense in early years and suits assets that are more productive when new. The carrying value is the cost less accumulated depreciation; it is the part of the cost not yet expensed.

Every transaction affects at least two accounts, and the accounting equation stays in balance: Assets = Liabilities + Owner’s Equity. Debit entries increase assets and expenses; credit entries increase liabilities, owner’s equity and revenue. Drawings reduce owner’s equity, so drawings increase with a debit.
check: Does an increase in an expense go on the debit or credit side?
The debit side.

p: A van costs $33,000 including GST, plus $1,000 (excluding GST) for signwriting. Residual value $4,000; useful life 5 years.
Cost = 30,000 + 1,000 = $31,000. Annual straight-line depreciation = (31,000 − 4,000) ÷ 5 = $5,400. After two years, accumulated depreciation is $10,800 and the carrying value is $20,200.

notes.h: Worked example: an Account Receivable record
p: Customer: T. Nguyen, terms 30 days. 1 April balance $440. 6 April credit sale, invoice 51, $880 including GST. 9 April T. Nguyen returns goods, credit note 7, $110 including GST. 20 April receipt 204, $440.
Balance after each entry: 440; then 440 + 880 = 1,320; then 1,320 − 110 = 1,210; then 1,210 − 440 = $770 owing at 30 April. The amounts include GST, because that is what the customer actually owes.
check: A customer owes $660, buys a further $1,100 on credit and pays $500. What is the balance?

p: Credit terms state how long the customer has to pay, for example “net 30 days”. Terms such as “5/7, n/30” offer a 5% discount for payment within 7 days, with the full amount due in 30. An ageing analysis lists what each customer owes by how long it has been outstanding: current, 30 to 60 days, over 60 days. The older a debt, the less likely it is to be collected, so old balances are followed up first.

notes.h: Depreciation: both methods side by side
p: A machine costs $20,000, has a residual value of $2,000 and a useful life of 4 years.
Straight-line: (20,000 − 2,000) ÷ 4 = $4,500 every year. Carrying value after year 1: $15,500; year 2: $11,000; year 3: $6,500; year 4: $2,000.

Reducing balance at 40% per annum: year 1: 40% × 20,000 = $8,000, carrying value $12,000. Year 2: 40% × 12,000 = $4,800, carrying value $7,200. Year 3: 40% × 7,200 = $2,880, carrying value $4,320. The expense is larger in early years and falls each year. Residual value is not subtracted before applying the rate.
Part of a year: if the machine was bought on 1 October and the period ends 31 December, straight-line depreciation is 4,500 × 3/12 = $1,125.
check: Equipment cost $12,000, residual value $2,000, useful life 5 years. What is the annual straight-line depreciation?

fig.cap: A $20,000 machine: straight-line depreciation ($4,500 a year to a $2,000 residual) against reducing balance at 40%, which falls fastest in the first year.

p: The asset helps earn revenue over several periods, so its cost is matched against that revenue over the same periods (accrual basis). Without depreciation, profit would be overstated every year the asset is used, and the asset would be overstated in the Balance Sheet.

Including GST in the cost of the asset. Forgetting to subtract the residual value. Depreciating for a full year when the asset was owned for only part of the reporting period: multiply by the fraction of the year.

topics.title: The three reports and their headings
points: Build order: Cash Flow Statement (closing Bank) → Income Statement (Net Profit) → Balance Sheet.
Cash Flow Statement for a period: Cash Flows from Operating, Investing and Financing Activities; Net Increase (Decrease) in cash position; Add Bank Balance at start; Bank Balance at end.
Income Statement for a period: Revenue; Less Cost of Goods Sold; Gross Profit; Less Inventory loss; Adjusted Gross Profit; Add Other revenue; Less Other expenses; Net Profit.
Balance Sheet as at a date: Assets (Current, Non-Current) | Equities (Current Liabilities, Non-Current Liabilities, Owner’s equity: Capital + Net Profit − Drawings). Total Assets = Total Equities.
Current = within the next 12 months. Interest is operating; loan principal and drawings are financing; buying a non-current asset is investing.
The Income Statement is GST-exclusive. Credit sales, depreciation and inventory loss are not cash flows.
topics.explain: Explain why a business can show a Net Profit but a decrease in cash.

qs.q: Repaying a loan’s principal is which cash flow?
Which heading belongs to the Balance Sheet?
o: Net Cash Flows from Operating Activities

qs.q: Sales $7 000, Cost of Sales $4 200, inventory loss $50, expenses $2 220. Find Net Profit.
qs.a: Gross Profit 2 800 → Adjusted GP 2 750 → Net Profit 530

qs.q: Capital $20 000, Net Profit $530, Drawings $500. Find closing owner’s equity.
Reports for a period use “for”. The Balance Sheet uses…
A cash purchase of equipment appears in the Cash Flow Statement under…
Sales $50,000; Cost of Goods Sold $28,000; other expenses $15,000. Find the Net Profit.
Opening capital $40,000, Net Profit $7,000, drawings $9,000. Find closing capital.

p: Before this lesson you should be able to record transactions in journals and inventory cards and calculate depreciation.

The big idea: records are for the bookkeeper; reports are for the owner. Three reports turn the period’s records into answers about cash, profit and financial position. Learning what belongs in each, and what does not, is the core skill of Units 1 and 2.

The Cash Flow Statement answers: where did cash come from and where did it go? The Income Statement answers: did the business earn more than it consumed? The Balance Sheet answers: what does the business control and owe at this date? An owner needs all three, because a business can be profitable and still run out of cash.

Operating activities are the cash flows from day-to-day trading: cash sales, receipts from Accounts Receivable, payments for inventory and to Accounts Payable, wages, other expenses, interest and GST. Investing activities are cash paid for, or received from the sale of, non-current assets. Financing activities are cash flows that change the size of the owner’s capital or borrowings: capital contributions, loans received, loan repayments and cash drawings.

Revenue is recognised when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, whether or not cash has moved. A credit sale is revenue on the day of the sale. Depreciation is an expense with no cash flow. Loan principal repayments, drawings, capital contributions and purchases of non-current assets never appear in the Income Statement.

An asset is a present economic resource controlled by the business as a result of past events. A liability is a present obligation to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events. Owner’s equity is the residual interest in the assets after deducting the liabilities. Current items are expected to be converted to cash, sold, consumed or settled within 12 months; everything else is non-current.
A loan often needs splitting: the part due in the next 12 months is a current liability and the remainder is non-current.
check: A $24,000 loan is repaid at $500 a month. How is it classified in the Balance Sheet?
$6,000 (the next 12 months) is a current liability and $18,000 is a non-current liability.

notes.h: Worked example: profit is not cash
p: In June a business makes cash sales of $8,000 and credit sales of $6,000 (cost of all inventory sold $7,000), pays wages of $2,000, records depreciation of $500, and repays $3,000 of loan principal.

Net Profit = (8,000 + 6,000) − 7,000 − 2,000 − 500 = $4,500. Cash from these items = 8,000 − 2,000 − 3,000 = $3,000, before any payment for the inventory itself. The credit sales raised profit without bringing in cash, depreciation reduced profit without using cash, and the loan repayment used cash without affecting profit.

Cash sales: operating cash inflow, and revenue. Credit sales: revenue, and an Account Receivable (current asset) until collected; no cash flow yet. Receipts from Accounts Receivable: operating cash inflow; not revenue (already recorded). Wages paid: operating cash outflow, and an expense. Depreciation: an expense only. Purchase of a vehicle for cash: investing cash outflow, and a non-current asset; not an expense. Loan received: financing cash inflow, and a liability. Loan repayment: financing cash outflow, reducing the liability; the interest is an operating outflow and an expense. Capital contribution: financing inflow, and owner’s equity. Drawings: financing outflow, reducing owner’s equity.
check: Where does the purchase of shop fittings for cash appear in the Cash Flow Statement?
Under Investing activities, as a cash outflow.

notes.h: Worked example: three reports from one set of data
p: A new business, for the month of July. Owner contributed $20,000. Took a $10,000 loan. Bought a van for $15,000 cash (ignore GST for simplicity). Bought inventory for cash $8,000. Cash sales $9,000 and credit sales $3,000; the cost of the inventory sold was $6,000. Paid wages $2,000 and rent $1,000. Depreciation of van $250. Drawings $500.

Cash Flow Statement. Operating: cash sales 9,000 − inventory 8,000 − wages 2,000 − rent 1,000 = −$2,000. Investing: van −$15,000. Financing: capital 20,000 + loan 10,000 − drawings 500 = +$29,500. Net increase in cash = $12,500, which is the closing bank balance.
Income Statement. Sales 12,000 − Cost of Sales 6,000 = Gross Profit $6,000. Less wages 2,000, rent 1,000, depreciation 250. Net Profit = $2,750.

Balance Sheet as at 31 July. Assets: Bank 12,500; Accounts Receivable 3,000; Inventory 2,000 (8,000 bought − 6,000 sold); Van 15,000 less accumulated depreciation 250 = 14,750. Total $32,250. Liabilities: Loan 10,000. Owner’s equity: Capital 20,000 + Net Profit 2,750 − Drawings 500 = 22,250. Total $32,250. The business made a profit while its operating cash flow was negative, because it spent cash on inventory that is still on hand and has not yet collected its credit sales.
check: Capital at start $30,000, Net Profit $8,000, Drawings $5,000. What is closing owner’s equity?

p: Headings without a period or date: the Income Statement and Cash Flow Statement are “for the period ended”, the Balance Sheet is “as at”. Putting drawings in the Income Statement. Classifying the whole loan as non-current. Listing GST received as revenue.

topics.title: Performance indicators
points: Profitability: ROI = Net Profit ÷ Average Capital × 100; ROA = Net Profit ÷ Average Total Assets × 100; Asset Turnover = Net Sales ÷ Average Total Assets; NPM = Net Profit ÷ Net Sales × 100; GPM = Gross Profit ÷ Net Sales × 100.
Liquidity: WCR = Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities; QAR = (CA − inventory − prepaid) ÷ CL; Cash Flow Cover = Net Cash Flow from Operating ÷ Average CL.
Speed: Inventory Turnover = Average Inventory ÷ COGS × 365; AR Turnover = Average AR ÷ Net Credit Sales (+GST) × 365; AP Turnover = Average AP ÷ Net Credit Purchases (+GST) × 365.
Stability: Debt Ratio = Total Liabilities ÷ Total Assets × 100.
Average = (start + end) ÷ 2. Compare with the previous period, budget and industry average.
Advice: what happened (with numbers) → why → effect → a specific recommendation.
topics.explain: Explain what a falling Net Profit Margin with a steady Gross Profit Margin tells you.

qs.q: Current Assets $18 000, Current Liabilities $12 000. Find the Working Capital Ratio.
Net Profit $8 000, Net Sales $50 000. Find NPM.
AR Turnover rises from 30 to 45 days. This means…
Which indicator measures stability?
Gross Profit is $30,000 and Net Sales are $120,000. Find the Gross Profit Margin.
Current assets are $45,000 and current liabilities $30,000. Find the Working Capital Ratio.
Average Accounts Receivable is $11,000 and credit sales including GST are $132,000. Find the Accounts Receivable Turnover in days.
qs.a: About 30 days
s: AR Turnover = Average AR ÷ Credit sales (incl. GST) × 365.

qs.q: An increasing Debt Ratio means the business…

p: Before this lesson you should be able to read an Income Statement and a Balance Sheet.

The big idea: reports give dollar amounts, but a $50,000 profit means something different for a corner shop than for a supermarket. Indicators turn amounts into ratios and percentages so that performance can be compared over time, against a budget and against other businesses. The calculation is the easy part; marks come from explaining what it shows.

A single figure means little. Compare it with something: the previous period (trend), the budget (benchmark the owner set), or a similar business (inter-business comparison). Then explain the cause by looking at the parts of the formula, and suggest an action. A complete answer has three steps: state the change with figures, explain why it happened, and say what it means for the business.

Profitability is the ability to earn profit, compared against a base such as sales, assets or the owner’s investment. Return on Owner’s Investment shows the return on the owner’s capital, which the owner compares with other investments. Return on Assets shows how well assets are used to earn profit. Asset Turnover shows how well assets generate sales. Gross Profit Margin shows the average mark-up being achieved; it changes only if selling prices or the cost prices of inventory change. Net Profit Margin shows how much of each sales dollar is left as profit, so it also reflects expense control.
If the Gross Profit Margin is steady but the Net Profit Margin has fallen, the cause must be other expenses rising faster than sales, or other revenue falling.

Liquidity is the ability to meet short-term debts as they fall due. A Working Capital Ratio below 1 means current liabilities exceed current assets. A very high ratio can also be a problem, because it may mean idle cash, excess inventory or slow-paying customers. The Quick Asset Ratio removes inventory and prepaid expenses, the current assets that are slowest to convert to cash, to test immediate liquidity.

Inventory Turnover measures the average number of days to sell inventory. Accounts Receivable Turnover measures the average days customers take to pay, to compare with the credit terms offered. Accounts Payable Turnover measures the average days the business takes to pay suppliers, to compare with the terms received. Faster inventory and receivable turnover improves liquidity.

The Debt Ratio shows the percentage of assets funded by liabilities. A higher ratio means more reliance on borrowing, more interest and more risk if profits fall. Debt can still be worthwhile if the return on the borrowed funds is higher than the interest.
Net Profit Margin fell from 12% to 9% while Gross Profit Margin stayed at 40% and sales rose 5%.

Answer: the business kept 3 cents less profit from each sales dollar. Since the Gross Profit Margin did not change, the mark-up was maintained, so the fall is due to poorer expense control: other expenses grew by more than the 5% growth in sales. The owner should compare each expense with the previous period and with budget to find which increased.

Indicators only measure what is recorded in dollars. Customer satisfaction, staff turnover, product quality, the number of returns, competitors’ actions and the state of the economy all help explain results and are often asked for.

notes.h: Worked example: calculating a set of indicators
p: Data for the year: Net Sales $200,000 (all on credit); Cost of Goods Sold $120,000; Net Profit $20,000. Average total assets $100,000; average capital $50,000. Current assets $40,000, including inventory $22,000 and prepaid expenses $2,000; current liabilities $25,000. Total liabilities $45,000; total assets $105,000. Average inventory $20,000; average Accounts Receivable $22,000.

Gross Profit Margin = 80,000 ÷ 200,000 = 40%. Net Profit Margin = 20,000 ÷ 200,000 = 10%. Return on Assets = 20,000 ÷ 100,000 = 20%. Asset Turnover = 200,000 ÷ 100,000 = 2 times. Return on Owner’s Investment = 20,000 ÷ 50,000 = 40%.

Working Capital Ratio = 40,000 ÷ 25,000 = 1.6 : 1. Quick Asset Ratio = (40,000 − 22,000 − 2,000) ÷ 25,000 = 0.64 : 1. Debt Ratio = 45,000 ÷ 105,000 = 43%. Inventory Turnover = 20,000 ÷ 120,000 × 365 = 61 days. Accounts Receivable Turnover = 22,000 ÷ 220,000 × 365 = 37 days (credit sales plus GST).
check: Net Profit $15,000 and Net Sales $120,000. What is the Net Profit Margin?

p: Each dollar of sales earns 40 cents of gross profit and 10 cents of net profit, so 30 cents goes on other expenses. The owner earns 40% on their investment, far better than a bank deposit, partly because nearly half the assets are funded by borrowing.

Liquidity is mixed. The Working Capital Ratio of 1.6 suggests the business can cover its short-term debts, but the Quick Asset Ratio of 0.64 shows it depends on selling inventory to do so, and inventory takes 61 days to sell. Customers take 37 days to pay; if the credit terms are 30 days, collection needs attention.
check: A business has a Working Capital Ratio of 2.5 but a Quick Asset Ratio of 0.5. What does this suggest?
Most of its current assets are inventory or prepaid expenses. It may struggle to pay debts quickly unless it can sell its inventory.

p: A trend compares this period with earlier periods of the same business and shows the direction of change. A budget comparison shows whether the owner’s own target was met. An inter-business comparison, against a similar business or an industry average, shows whether performance is competitive. A result can be improving and still be below the industry average, so use more than one benchmark.
check: Name the three benchmarks used to assess an indicator.
Previous periods (trend), the budget, and a similar business or industry average.

p: Saying a ratio is “good” or “bad” with no benchmark. Using closing figures where the formula needs an average. Forgetting to add GST to credit sales for Accounts Receivable Turnover. Stating that faster turnover is better without saying why it helps cash flow. Describing the change and stopping before explaining its cause.

topics.title: Assumptions, characteristics, budgets and ethics
points: Assumptions: Accounting entity (business separate from owner), Accrual basis (record when earned or incurred), Going concern (will keep operating), Period (equal reporting periods).
Qualitative characteristics: Relevance, Faithful representation, Comparability, Verifiability, Timeliness, Understandability.
Budgets plan, control and evaluate. Variance: favourable if revenue is above or an expense below budget; unfavourable otherwise.
Selling price = cost × (1 + mark-up ÷ 100). CVP: quantity = (fixed costs + profit) ÷ (selling price − variable cost per unit).
Ethical, social and environmental considerations: honest reports, fair treatment of suppliers and staff, waste and sustainability.
topics.explain: Explain which assumption is broken when an owner pays a family holiday from the business account and records it as an expense.

qs.q: Recording a credit sale as revenue before the cash arrives follows…
Information that can be checked against source documents is…
Fixed costs $400, selling price $50, variable cost $30. How many units to break even?
Budgeted wages $1 000, actual $1 200. State the variance.
qs.a: $200 Unfavourable

qs.q: Recording a credit sale as revenue when the invoice is issued applies the…
Fixed costs are $9,000, the selling price is $30 and the variable cost is $18 per unit. Find the break-even point.
qs.a: 750 units

qs.q: The owner pays her personal phone bill from the business account. Recording it as drawings follows the…
Budgeted wages are $8,000 and actual wages are $8,600. State the variance.
qs.a: $600 unfavourable
qs.e: The expense was higher than budgeted.

p: Before this lesson it helps to have worked through recording and reporting, because the theory explains why those tasks are done the way they are.

The big idea: accounting follows a shared set of rules so that reports mean the same thing to everyone who reads them. Four assumptions say how reports are prepared, and six qualitative characteristics say what makes the information useful. Theory questions ask you to connect a real situation to these rules.

The assumptions are the ground rules for preparing reports. Accounting entity: the business is separate from its owner and from other businesses, so only the business’s transactions are recorded; this is why the owner taking cash is drawings and not wages. Going concern: the business is assumed to continue operating into the future, which allows assets and liabilities to be classified as current or non-current and assets to be recorded at cost. Period: the life of the business is divided into periods of equal length so that profit can be measured and compared. Accrual basis: revenues are recognised when earned and expenses when incurred, so profit is calculated by matching the two in the same period.

The characteristics describe what makes financial information useful. Relevance: information is capable of making a difference to a decision; this includes materiality, meaning its omission could influence the decision. Faithful representation: information is complete, neutral (free from bias) and free from material error. Verifiability: different knowledgeable observers could reach the same conclusion, supported by source documents. Comparability: reports can be compared over time and between businesses, which needs consistent methods. Timeliness: information is available in time to influence decisions. Understandability: information is presented clearly and concisely.

Characteristics can pull against each other. Waiting for a verified figure improves faithful representation but reduces timeliness. In an answer, name the characteristic, define it, then apply it to the case in the question.

Example: the owner wants to record a new delivery van at the $40,000 they believe it is worth, although the invoice shows $35,000. The $35,000 should be used. It is verifiable because it is supported by the invoice, and it is a faithful representation because it is free from bias. The owner’s estimate is not supported by evidence.

A budget is a prediction of future transactions. It assists planning by showing likely cash shortages or profit, and it provides a benchmark to compare with actual results. A variance report shows each difference and whether it is favourable or unfavourable.

Break-even is the level of sales where total revenue equals total costs. Contribution margin per unit = selling price − variable cost per unit. Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit. Margin of safety is the amount by which actual or budgeted sales exceed break-even sales.
Fixed costs $12,000; selling price $50; variable cost $30. Contribution margin = $20, so break-even = 12,000 ÷ 20 = 600 units. To earn a $4,000 profit: (12,000 + 4,000) ÷ 20 = 800 units.

Ethical considerations are about doing the right thing by owners, staff, customers, suppliers, the community and the environment. Typical exam cases: choosing a cheaper supplier with poor labour practices, delaying payments to small suppliers, or leaving information out of a report. A good answer weighs the financial effect against the ethical one and reaches a recommendation.
Use three steps: identify, define, apply. Identify the assumption or characteristic. Define it in a sentence. Apply it to the facts in the question, using the names and amounts given.

Example question: the owner paid her home electricity bill from the business bank account and wants it recorded as a business expense. Answer: “This should be recorded as drawings, not as an expense. Under the accounting entity assumption, the business is separate from its owner, and only business transactions are recorded in its reports. The home electricity is a personal expense of the owner, so recording it as a business expense would understate profit and would not be a faithful representation of the business’s expenses.”
check: The owner wants to leave a large unpaid electricity bill out of this year’s expenses because it has not been paid yet. Which assumption does this breach?
The accrual basis assumption: expenses are recognised when incurred, not when paid.

p: Recording a sale when the invoice is issued, before cash arrives: accrual basis. Splitting a loan into current and non-current: going concern. Preparing reports every month or year: period. Keeping the owner’s car out of the Balance Sheet: accounting entity.

Using the invoice amount, not an estimate: verifiability and faithful representation. Using the same depreciation method each year: comparability. Giving the owner the report soon after the period ends: timeliness. Using clear headings and a graph: understandability. Reporting a large inventory loss separately instead of hiding it in Cost of Sales: relevance.
check: Which qualitative characteristic is supported by keeping source documents for every transaction?
Verifiability.

p: Budgeted sales $50,000, actual $46,000: variance $4,000 unfavourable. Budgeted wages $12,000, actual $11,000: variance $1,000 favourable. Budgeted advertising $2,000, actual $800: variance $1,200 favourable.

A discussion would link them: spending much less than planned on advertising, and less on wages, may be the reason sales fell short. The favourable expense variances did not make up for the lost sales, so the overall result is worse than budget.

notes.h: Break-even: a second example and a graph
p: A café sells coffee at $5. Each cup costs $1.50 in beans, milk and cup. Fixed costs are $2,800 a week. Contribution margin = 5 − 1.50 = $3.50 per cup. Break-even = 2,800 ÷ 3.50 = 800 cups a week. If the café sells 1,000 cups, the margin of safety is 200 cups, and profit = 200 × 3.50 = $700.

On a break-even graph, the total cost line starts at the level of fixed costs and rises with each unit; the revenue line starts at zero and rises more steeply. They cross at the break-even point. Below it the gap is a loss; above it the gap is profit. If the selling price rises, the revenue line gets steeper and the break-even point falls.
check: Selling price $20, variable cost $12, fixed costs $4,000. How many units must be sold to break even?

fig.cap: Café break-even: revenue $5 per cup against total cost $2,800 + $1.50 per cup. They cross at 800 cups; above that is profit.

p: Naming a concept without defining or applying it. Confusing verifiability (can it be checked against evidence?) with faithful representation (is it complete, neutral and free from error?). Calling drawings an expense. Dividing fixed costs by the selling price in a break-even calculation instead of by the contribution margin.
